newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Gaza meeting cannot replace peace talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Gaza meeting cannot replace peace talks.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday an international meeting called by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was an important chance for him to air concerns but was no substitute for direct talks with Israel.

Arafat voiced hope on Wednesday that the meeting in Gaza on Saturday of U.S., European and Arab envoys would rescue Middle East peace from a crisis over Israeli policies. Israel has criticised the meeting.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "This is an opportunity for the Palestinians to express their concerns about the present situation in the Middle East and to hear the views of friendly countries like the United States."
"It's appropriate that we go," he added.
Washington upset its ally Israel on Tuesday by announcing that a senior American diplomat, consul general in Jerusalem Edward Abington, would attend the gathering.
Israel is worried that Arafat will use the meeting to assemble a worldwide coalition to press the Jewish state into concessions.
But Burns told a news briefing the United States "does not see this meeting as a forum for decisions on the Middle East peace issues or as a negotiating session."
"Nor do we view it as an alternative to the direct negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians that to this date have produced the progress that we all know about in the Middle East," he added.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk at a meeting on Wednesday of his country's displeasure at the U.S. decision to attend.

The decision also came under fire from 13 Democratic members of the U.S. House of Representatives, who said in a letter to President Bill Clinton that it would be "a serious mistake ... to participate in such a one-sided meeting."
"The U.S. must not jeopardise its role as a mediator by sending a representative to this meeting," said the signatories, eight of them from New York.

Analysts said there was little doubt that Washington's move was intended to underline U.S. criticisms of recent Israeli decisions to start a Jewish housing project in Arab East Jerusalem and to close Palestinian offices there.
Burns said such decisions were "difficult to explain to the Palestinian people" and it made sense for the Palestinians to hold the kind of meeting that Arafat has convened.
He said Washington was aware of Israeli unhappiness, but added: "Our advice to the Palestinians and Israelis is, you need to get beyond a war of words."
The U.S. spokesman also appealed to King Hussein of Jordan and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to patch up a dispute that led to a heated exchange of letters this week.
Hussein warned Netanyahu against high-handed treatment of the Palestinians and said he could no longer consider the Israeli leader a serious peace partner.
Burns said both men were friends of the United States.

"They obviously have their differences on some issues, but we hope that Jordan and Israel will continue to be friends and that the issues that they need to work out are worked out between them," he said.

Burns appeared to voice concern over a statement on Wednesday by Hussein, who is due to meet Clinton in Washington next week, that there was "a very strong chance of violence" if Israel pursued its housing plan.
Without mentioning Hussein, Burns said, "You have to be very careful when you talk about violence. Violence is a language of the past in the Middle East."
